name: collecting-parameter
intent: Let several callees contribute to one result by passing a mutable accumulator through the call tree, so no callee has to return an intermediate value that the caller then merges.
problem: A result is assembled from many small producers: if every callee returns its own collection the caller must merge results level by level, while keeping the partial result in a field or global makes the accumulation state ambient, shared across invocations and hard to test.
context: Local code structure inside one object or module - rendering, parsing, validation, traversal or reporting code - where a call tree of small methods each produces part of a single result and one owner can create the accumulator, keep it alive for the walk and consume it when the walk returns.
benefits: One accumulation site: the caller chooses the concrete result type (list, string builder, map, report) and the append policy (order, deduplication, separators) once, instead of each callee inventing and merging its own intermediate.
No per-frame merge ceremony: a deeply nested or recursive producer contributes without returning, unwrapping and combining a collection at every level of the call tree.
The working state is an explicit parameter rather than an instance field or global, so re-entrant and recursive calls can each carry their own accumulator.
Producer signatures become uniform and small ('append this part into the sink'), which keeps each callee single-purpose and lets a visitor or traversal dispatch to them mechanically.
Appending is amortised O(1) into an existing container, avoiding the intermediate allocations and copies of a build-and-merge style.
Accumulators compose naturally with recursive traversals: a helper function carries the accumulator down the recursion, enabling true tail recursion in languages where it matters.
The pattern is library/framework-friendly: a framework can provide the accumulator (e.g., a receiver interface) and client code appends to it without knowing the final collection type.
tradeoffs: The mutation is invisible in the signature: a method whose parameter is appended to still looks like a query, so the append contract must be carried by naming, documentation and convention.

The accumulator must outlive the whole call tree and must not be aliased or replaced: a re-assigned parameter (out = out + x), a copy of a value-type accumulator, or a temporary handed to a deferred or asynchronous producer silently drops contributions.
Append order and multiplicity become an implicit contract between callees that the compiler cannot check; duplicated or re-ordered contributions surface only in the final result.
Contributors are harder to test and reuse in isolation: a test must construct, inspect and understand the accumulator type instead of comparing return values.
A single accumulator serialises concurrent producers (they need locking or interleaving) and grows with the whole result, so it is a poor fit for streaming, unbounded output or parallel reduction.
In lazy or functional languages, an accumulating parameter that is not strict can accumulate thunks rather than values, causing stack overflow even in tail-recursive forms.

participants.responsibility: Creates the accumulator, decides its concrete type and append protocol, drives the collaboration and is the only role allowed to read or consume the collected result.
The mutable accumulator that owns the partially built result for the duration of the collaboration; it is passed unchanged to every contributor and returned to no one.
Any method that appends its own part to the parameter and knows nothing else about it - no reading back, no clearing, no replacement.
A traversal or recursive driver that receives the parameter and passes the same instance on to nested contributors, keeping the accumulator identity stable across the whole call tree.

use_cases: Text, HTML or XML generation where a walk over a tree or a sequence of methods writes fragments into one output buffer or string builder.
Parsing and static analysis: a recursive-descent parser or visiting pass appends diagnostics, warnings or AST nodes to one list while walking, instead of returning a list per production.
Test-result gathering: JUnit's TestResult is the canonical example - each test is run with a result object passed in and appends its failures and errors to it (c2 wiki).
Building an index or registry during a traversal: a visitor collects nodes under a key into one map without every visit returning a partial map.
Reporting and aggregation over heterogeneous nodes (counts, sums, rule violations) where each node type appends its own contribution to one report object.

Library and framework SPIs: Gunnar Morling's 'Emitter Parameter Pattern' — a framework provides a receiver interface and client code appends results without instantiating return objects; enables streaming, uniform handling of single/multiple values, and non-breaking SPI evolution.
Java Stream reduction: the Stream.collect(Collector) API is a first-class formalisation of this pattern, with supplier, accumulator, combiner and finisher functions.
Event or log aggregation: a handler chain appends events to a shared buffer as a request or message flows through the pipeline.
Validation error accumulation: collecting all validation failures in one pass rather than failing on the first error.
Recursive tree operations where intermediate results from subtrees must be merged (e.g., computing a bill-of-materials total, aggregating statistics across a filesystem tree).

Roslyn (C# compiler): a DiagnosticBag is threaded through the binder and analyzer pipeline - each binding or analysis pass appends diagnostics via Add/AddRange instead of returning a list per pass - and the driver seals the bag into an immutable array with ToReadOnly when the compilation completes.

Go standard library: the io.Writer parameter of fmt.Fprintf/Fprintln and json.NewEncoder(w) is the canonical sink - renderers and encoders write fragments into the caller-supplied writer instead of returning strings, and writers compose via io.MultiWriter or a bytes.Buffer.

TypeScript compiler: the type checker pushes errors and suggestions into a shared diagnostics array through addDiagnostic during its traversal of the AST rather than every check function returning its own diagnostic list.
avoid_when: Only one producer computes the result: return the value (Interesting Return Value) instead of adding an output parameter.
The result is a map/filter/fold over one collection: a collection pipeline returns the result directly and is shorter and safer.
The accumulation state genuinely belongs to the object across calls: keep it as an instance field (or use a Method Object) rather than passing it on every call.
Producers may run concurrently or the output is unbounded: use per-producer results plus an explicit merge, a concurrent collector, or streaming instead of one shared accumulator.
pitfalls: Appenders reading, clearing or re-ordering the accumulator break the single-owner contract that made the pattern safe.
A shared accumulator reused across invocations accumulates stale results; give every traversal its own instance.
No thread-safety: concurrent producers need per-producer accumulators plus a merge, or a concurrent collector type.

Value-type accumulators (int, struct, list in some languages) are copied on pass-by-value; contributors append to the copy, silently losing contributions — pass by reference or use a mutable heap-allocated container.
Deferred or asynchronous execution (callbacks, promises, futures) that outlives the synchronous call tree retains a reference to a parameter that has already been consumed or invalidated.

In lazy languages, accumulating into a thunk chain instead of a strict accumulator causes stack overflow; use strict evaluation ($! in Haskell, seq in strict languages) to force the accumulator at each step.
Re-assigning the accumulator parameter (e.g., out = out + item) severs the connection to the original container; the caller sees an empty result.

Wrong move: pass one shared accumulator through a parallel or async pipeline -> contributions interleave, duplicate, or arrive after the result was consumed -> instead give each worker its own accumulator and merge deterministically at the join (java.util.stream.Collector's combiner contract) or use a concurrent collector type.

Wrong move: have an appending method both mutate and return the accumulator -> callers start re-assigning or branching on the returned value and fork the accumulation away from the original container -> instead keep contributors append-only and returning nothing, with consumption confined to the single owner.

Wrong move: bind the accumulator as a default argument (def collect(node, out=[]) in Python) -> the one default list persists across calls and silently accumulates earlier runs' results -> instead default to None and create a fresh accumulator inside, or require the caller to pass one explicitly.
anti_patterns: Bidirectional parameter: passing an object whose properties callees both read and write as the collaboration proceeds - called out on the c2 wiki itself as generally an anti-pattern because it creates hidden stateful coupling between methods.
Using an output parameter merely to avoid writing a return value, leaving callers to construct a container and inspect it where a returned value would read better.
Sharing one accumulator across threads, tasks or re-entrant invocations without a concurrent type or per-invocation instances, producing interleaved or duplicated content.
Letting contributors read, clear or reorder the accumulator (or handing it to code that does), so the caller loses the single-owner contract that made the pattern safe.
design_principles: Single responsibility: contributors produce their part; the client owns assembly and the final shape of the result.
Explicit state over ambient state: state that would otherwise live in a field or global is passed as a visible parameter.
Information hiding: contributors depend on the narrowest append protocol (add/append/write), not on the concrete container.
Deliberate command-query separation: a method that appends should not also return the accumulator, or the mutation becomes invisible twice over.
best_practices: Create the accumulator at the single place that knows the final shape; pass the same instance down the call tree and consume it there.
Type the parameter to the narrowest protocol the contributors need (Appendable, io.Writer, an add method) rather than the concrete class.
Name the parameter for direction ('out', 'into', 'sink', 'collector', 'receiver') and state in the method's documentation that it appends and in what order.
Keep contributors append-only; treat any read, clear or re-order of the accumulator inside a producer as a design smell.
Give each invocation its own accumulator, and merge explicitly (or use a concurrent collector) when producers can run in parallel; never reuse an accumulator across runs without clearing it.
Invalidate or close the accumulator after consumption so that any accidental post-consumption append raises an error rather than silently appending to a stale or shared buffer.
In lazy languages, force strict evaluation of the accumulator at each step to prevent thunk chains that cause stack overflow; in Haskell use seq or $!.
In recursive traversals, model the accumulator invariant explicitly: document what the accumulator represents at each call depth so the base case and update logic are verifiably correct.

When building a collecting parameter for an SPI or library API, expose only an interface for the receiver type; the framework controls the concrete accumulator, enabling non-breaking evolution (new append methods, streaming, or re-use).
For deeply nested or many-callee collaborations, consider pairing this pattern with a Forwarder role so that contributors receive the accumulator without needing to know its concrete type.
sources: Beck, K., Smalltalk Best Practice Patterns, Prentice Hall (1997), Behavior chapter, pp. 75-77: 'To return a collection that is the collaborative result of several methods, add a parameter to all the methods that collects the results.'

Rising, L., Patterns Almanac (Linda Rising) - records Collecting Parameter from Beck at pages 75-77.
Kerivsky, J., Refactoring to Patterns, ch. 'Move Accumulation to Collecting Parameter' (Industrial Logic) - applies the pattern as a refactoring target to replace inline accumulation.

Morling, G., 'The Emitter Parameter Pattern for Flexible SPI Contracts' (2020), https://www.morling.dev/blog/emitter-parameter-pattern-for-flexible-spis/ - modernises the pattern for library/framework SPI design, identifies single/multiple value handling, flexible SPI evolution, and streaming as key advantages.

Felleisen et al., How to Design Programs (HTDP), Part VI 'Accumulators' - formal treatment of accumulator invariants, recognition of when accumulation is needed, and transformation of structurally recursive functions into accumulator style.
https://wiki.haskell.org/Performance/Accumulating_parameter - 'Accumulating Parameters: Getting rid of the almost in tail recursive', shows strictness technique to prevent thunk chains.

Walling, T., 'Roundabout, A Pattern Language for Recursive Programming', University of North Carolina, Section 4 'Accumulator Variable' - explicitly maps Accumulator Variable to Beck's Collecting Parameter and connects it to Interface Procedure.

Oracle, Java SE Documentation, java.util.stream.Collector - the mutable reduction contract formalising supplier, accumulator, combiner and finisher functions; includes CONCURRENT characteristic for lock-free parallel accumulation.
Oracle, Java SE Documentation, java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAccumulator and DoubleAccumulator - thread-safe accumulating parameters for numeric reduction under high contention.

Microsoft Learn, '.NET Thread-Safe Collections', System.Collections.Concurrent - concurrent collection classes enabling safe multi-producer accumulation with fine-grained locking or lock-free Interlocked operations.

Turner, A., 'Aggregation Patterns C#: Reduce Operations in TPL', dotnetz2h.com - thread-local aggregation pattern: each thread accumulates into its own container, finalizer merges; avoids lock contention in parallel reduction.
Refactoring Guru, 'Builder Pattern' - contrasts step-by-step object construction (related accumulation, different goal) with the collecting parameter's single-pass fragment assembly.
Java Design Patterns, 'Collecting Parameter Pattern in Java' (java-design-patterns.com) - notes relationship with Command, Composite and Visitor patterns; provides printer-queue filtering example.

Chromium Docs, 'The Builder & Parameter Bundle Patterns' - parameter bundle as a named group of constructor arguments; related to collecting parameter in that both bundle multiple pieces into one passing operation.

Microsoft, dotnet/roslyn, https://github.com/dotnet/dotnet/blob/766c39a8f28bfdbfb61e7a6ed570b5e94c28c831/src/roslyn/src/Compilers/Core/Portable/Diagnostic/DiagnosticBag.cs - mutable thread-safe bag of diagnostics threaded through Roslyn's bind and analysis phases; Add/AddRange append during the walk and ToReadOnly seals the final immutable array.

Go Packages documentation, https://pkg.go.dev/io and https://pkg.go.dev/fmt - io.Writer as the append sink passed into Fprint/Fprintf/Fprintln and json.NewEncoder(w), the Go idiom for 'write your part into the caller's accumulator'; io.MultiWriter composes several sinks.

GitHub, microsoft/TypeScript-Compiler-Notes, codebase/src/compiler/checker.md - the diagnostics-producing type checker queues errors and suggestions via addDiagnostic during the AST traversal instead of returning them per check.

Stack Overflow, 'Is it best practice to use the Collecting Parameter pattern?' (https://stackoverflow.com/questions/57175045) - practitioner criticism: the invisible side effect and harder unit-testing mean reviewers prefer returned, composed values unless a genuinely shared sink simplifies the flow.
